children: The Federal Aviation Administration will delay certification of Boeing's latest 737 MAX model as air-safety regulators assess a new software glitch that some industry officials worry may pose a potential safety risk while landing, the agency chief said Monday.
Boeing has been seeking to win the FAA's approval for the MAX 10, the longest version of the 737 variant.

"We haven't concluded whether this is a safety-of-flight issue or not," FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said at a press conference Monday, when asked about the software glitch. "But we will be delaying the 10 until we're satisfied that we don't have an issue here."

The FAA hasn't telegraphed publicly when it had been planning to certify the aircraft, but industry and government officials have said regulators were expected to approve the 737 MAX 10 for passenger service as soon as October.
A Boeing spokesman said: "We continue to follow the lead of the FAA as we work through the certification process."

For Boeing, a safety setback could damage its efforts to restore trust with regulators, airline customers and the flying public after its 737 MAX was grounded for nearly two years after a pair of fatal crashes. The accidents led to scrutiny that delayed FAA approvals for newer versions of the jet.
Boeing's stock fell 6.9% Monday, its largest single-day drop since April 2025.

The FAA in August certified the smallest variant of the aircraft, the 737 MAX 7, with the software bug, and Bedford on Monday said those planes were nonetheless safe. He compared the glitch to a software bug with a phone or computer software update.
Unlike with a faulty flight-control system that played a major role in the earlier crashes, Bedford said this issue is significantly different.

"It doesn't take control away from the pilots," Bedford said. "The pilots remain in control of the airplane. They train for these scenarios. So I think the issue that we're looking at right now is the workload component under these more obscure situations and how we feel about that."
The Wall Street Journal reported over the weekend that Boeing had identified a glitch that could cause an automated navigation feature to fail.

The glitch, which Boeing acknowledged, emerged from a cockpit software update and can occur when flight crews alter their planned flight path following a missed approach. In a certain scenario, pilots may have to fly manually without some autopilot functions. That, some industry officials said, could overwork pilots while they are already busy, at low altitude and possibly dealing with situations like bad weather.
The company said it was working with airlines on a procedure to allow pilots to re-enable the automated navigation feature if needed, and devising a software fix.
The software in question was developed by GE Aerospace. The company didn't immediately comment Monday.
Bedford said such software updates often try to fix various issues with new versions.
"I think in this particular case, due to the focus that's on it, GE may try to get this software correction in much quicker," he said. "Is that weeks, days, months? It remains to be seen."
